result: SBFSEM imaging of L. mexicana-infected sand flies at 10 days post-infection revealed dense haptomonad colonization of the stomodeal valve with specific morphological characteristics. Haptomonads were present in layers on both sides of the valve, with flagellum length varying by distance from the surface. Attached cells had shorter, wider cell bodies compared to unattached cells, and the majority (83%) attached via the distal flagellar tip while 17% attached laterally. The axoneme in tip-attached cells extended only just beyond the cell body, whereas in laterally attached cells it extended further along the flagellum.
evaluation: Claims C17-C27 are well-supported by quantitative SBFSEM data with appropriate sample sizes (n=50 attached, n=39 unattached, n=17 lateral). The morphological measurements are presented with standard deviations and are directly observable in the imaging data. The spatial organization and structural details are consistently documented across multiple cells.

result: Cells with laterally attached flagella may represent transitional forms differentiating to or from the haptomonad stage, and most unattached cells and laterally attached cells had metacyclic/leptomonad morphology.
evaluation: Claims C28-C29 involve speculative interpretations of morphological observations. While the morphological data are sound, the inference about differentiation status is not directly demonstrated and represents a hypothesis based on intermediate morphological characteristics. The comparison to previous reports (C29) provides some support but does not definitively establish the differentiation state.

result: The vast majority of haptomonads were non-dividing (1N1F), but a small number of dividing forms (1N2F or 2N2F) were identified. In dividing cells with long new flagella, both flagella were attached, while in cells with short new flagella only the old flagellum was attached. Four abnormal cells with multiple nuclei but single flagella were also observed.
evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are supported by quantitative analysis of over 1000 cells from SBFSEM data. The observations are clearly documented with specific counts and are consistent with previous reports (C30 cites Gossage et al., 2003). The identification of dividing forms contradicts earlier suggestions that haptomonads are non-replicative, which is appropriately noted.

result: A small number of haptomonads (6 in ~1000 cells) showed partial or complete detachment from the stomodeal valve, potentially representing cells differentiating back to free-swimming forms. Detachment of the cuticular lining from epithelial cells was observed where many haptomonads were adhered.
evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by quantitative data, but C36 acknowledges alternative explanations (fixation artifacts). The interpretation that detached forms represent differentiation is speculative. Claim C37 is supported by observations consistent with previous studies, though the causal relationship between haptomonad adhesion and cuticular damage is not definitively established.

result: Electron tomography revealed detailed 3D ultrastructure of the haptomonad flagellum. The haptomonad attached via the distal flagellar tip with an electron-dense attachment plaque. The cell body had a shorter asymmetric extension with a wider anterior tip. The flagellar pocket had a shortened neck region with flagellar expansion and numerous junctional complexes. The flagellum contained a 9+2 axoneme extending just beyond the cell body with accessory structures (radial spokes, dynein arms) but lacked the paraflagellar rod (PFR).
evaluation: Claims C38-C45 are well-supported by high-resolution electron tomography data. The structural observations are detailed and quantitative (e.g., microtubule capping structures, absence of PFR). The use of Markham rotational averaging (C43) is an established method for analyzing axonemal structures. The observations are internally consistent and provide unprecedented detail of haptomonad ultrastructure.

result: The attachment plaque complex consisted of discrete structural layers: outer and inner dense plaques (~10 nm each) overlaying the flagellar membrane, connected to a dense filamentous layer (~100 nm). Filaments and filament bundles extended from the FAZ to the attachment interface over ~3 μm, appearing to connect the attachment interface to the cell body. The stomodeal valve had a layered structure including a putative wax layer (~10 nm). The flagellar membrane was positioned ~10 nm from the valve surface with connecting structures spanning this gap.
evaluation: Claims C46-C53 are supported by detailed electron tomography observations with quantitative measurements of layer thicknesses and distances. The structural organization is clearly documented in the imaging data. The identification of the wax layer (C50) is supported by comparison with literature on insect cuticle structure. The observations of connecting structures with consistent spacing provide strong evidence for specific transmembrane proteins.

result: The haptomonad flagellar membrane showed numerous projections and indentations. Large vesicular structures were observed throughout the flagellum, and smaller vesicles were seen near the attachment interface, with one appearing to fuse with or bud from the flagellar membrane.
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are directly supported by electron tomography observations. The vesicular structures are clearly visible in the imaging data. However, the interpretation of vesicle function (discussed in C101-C103) remains speculative.

result: In vitro haptomonad-like cells generated on scratched plastic substrates showed morphological and ultrastructural similarity to sand fly haptomonads. SEM and SBFSEM revealed cells with short, wide cell bodies and short flagella attached via attachment plaques. The in vitro cells had shortened flagella with 9+2 axonemes without PFR, expanded FAZ areas, and layered attachment plaque complexes similar to in vivo haptomonads. Quantitative morphological comparisons showed in vitro cells had slightly longer cell bodies but were otherwise similar in flagellum length, axoneme length, and cell body width. More dividing cells were observed in vitro than in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C57-C66 are well-supported by comparative SBFSEM and electron tomography data from in vitro and in vivo samples. Quantitative morphological measurements (C65) with statistical analysis demonstrate similarity between the two systems. The conclusion that in vitro forms are suitable for studying haptomonad biology (C66) is a reasonable inference based on the demonstrated structural similarities, though the caveat about potential differences is appropriately noted.

result: Time-lapse microscopy of in vitro haptomonad-like cell adhesion identified five distinct stages occurring over 2-9 hours: (1) surface exploration with flagellum and membrane streamer release, (2) initial flagellum adhesion at any point along its length, (3) stable attachment with potential flagellum loop formation (7/10 cells), (4) flagellum shortening with membrane expansion and fusion, and (5) attachment maturation with clear attachment plaque and cell body reorientation. Throughout adhesion, the cell body became shorter and wider.
evaluation: Claims C67-C77 are supported by time-lapse microscopy data from 8 videos showing 10 adhering cells. The five stages are clearly documented with specific observations at each stage. Quantitative data on flagellum loop formation (C73) strengthens the findings. SEM confirmation of the stages (C77) provides independent validation. The sample size is modest but adequate for this descriptive analysis.

result: Some adhesion attempts were unsuccessful (3/10 cells), with cells detaching and swimming away before flagellum disassembly, suggesting that the initial stages (1-3) of adhesion are reversible in vitro.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by quantitative observations from time-lapse microscopy. The inference about reversibility (C79) is reasonable based on the observed detachment events. However, the generalization is limited to in vitro conditions and the sample size is small.

result: Fluorescence microscopy of cells expressing tagged RSP4/6 and PFR2 showed that both signals shortened in parallel with flagellum shortening during adhesion. In mature haptomonad-like cells, only short RSP4/6 signal was consistently seen, while PFR2 signal was absent in 30% (9/30) of cells, suggesting PFR disassembly during adhesion.
evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by fluorescence microscopy data with quantitative analysis (n=30 cells for C81). The observations are consistent with the electron microscopy findings showing absence of PFR in haptomonads (C45). The inference about PFR disassembly (C82) is reasonable based on the loss of PFR2 signal.

result: In vitro purified metacyclics showed very low adhesion capacity compared to promastigotes after 24 hours.
evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by quantitative comparison of adhesion between promastigotes and metacyclics. The experimental design is appropriate with proper controls. However, the generalization to in vivo metacyclics requires caution as in vitro purified metacyclics may not fully represent the in vivo state.

result: EGTA (1-2 mM) had no effect on promastigote growth in suspension but dramatically reduced adhesion in a dose-dependent manner. In contrast, EGTA treatment of already-attached cells did not cause detachment. These results indicate that Ca2+ is critical for adhesion formation but not maintenance in Leishmania in vitro, contrasting with previous findings in T. congolense and suggesting different regulatory mechanisms for adhesion in different trypanosomatids.
evaluation: Claims C84-C90 are well-supported by experimental data with appropriate controls and replication (n=3 independent experiments). The dose-dependent effect of EGTA on adhesion formation (C85) and lack of effect on maintenance (C88) are clearly demonstrated. The comparison with T. congolense (C86) is appropriately cited, and the inference about different regulatory mechanisms (C87) is reasonable. Statistical analysis with p-values strengthens the conclusions.

result: The haptomonad attachment plaque has a layered architecture with inner and outer dense plaques connecting to a dense filament layer, similar in arrangement to mammalian hemidesmosomes. However, no orthologues of hemidesmosome constituent proteins are found in the L. mexicana genome.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by electron tomography observations (C91) and genomic analysis (C93). The structural similarity to hemidesmosomes (C92) is an appropriate inference based on morphology, and the authors correctly note the absence of protein orthologues, justifying their use of the term 'attachment plaque' rather than 'hemidesmosome.'

result: Filaments in the haptomonad flagellum are 8-10 nm thick, similar to intermediate or septin filaments in other eukaryotes, and filament bundles (16-20 nm) may be formed by bundling individual filaments. However, no orthologues of intermediate filament or septin proteins are present in the Leishmania genome, suggesting Leishmania may have unique filament-forming proteins.
evaluation: Claim C94 is supported by measurements from electron microscopy data. However, claims C95 and C97 are speculative inferences. While the absence of known filament protein orthologues (C96) is established, the conclusion about unique filament-forming proteins requires identification and characterization of the actual proteins involved, which is not provided in this study.

result: Connections spanning the ~10 nm gap between the flagellar membrane and stomodeal valve surface are more likely transmembrane proteins rather than flexible substances like mucus, based on their constant spacing and absence in wider gaps.
evaluation: Claim C98 is a reasonable inference based on the consistent spacing (~10 nm) of the connections and their absence in wider gaps. The logic is sound, though definitive identification of these structures as transmembrane proteins would require additional biochemical or proteomic analysis.

result: The haptomonad flagellum has undergone dramatic remodeling, with strong attachment mediated not only by the attachment plaque but also by numerous filaments and filament bundles connecting the attachment interface to the FAZ junctional complexes.
evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by the comprehensive structural observations from electron tomography. The conclusion about dramatic remodeling (C99) is justified by the documented changes in flagellar structure. The inference about the role of filaments in buttressing attachment (C100) is reasonable based on the observed structural organization.

result: Vesicles within the flagellum may represent mechanisms for flagellar membrane removal during disassembly. Smaller vesicles near the attachment interface may contain components for attachment plaque assembly or support exo/endocytosis for releasing factors like chitinase onto the stomodeal valve surface.
evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are speculative interpretations of the observed vesicles. While the vesicles are clearly documented (C55-C56), their function is not directly demonstrated. The analogy to desmosome assembly (C102) provides some support, but these remain hypotheses requiring experimental validation.

result: While most haptomonads were non-dividing, dividing forms were observed, potentially representing asymmetric differentiation divisions or proliferative divisions. In cells with long new flagella, both flagella were attached, suggesting proliferative division. In cells with short new flagella, only the old flagellum was attached, suggesting attachment structure formation is post-axonemal assembly and requires sufficient flagellum length.
evaluation: Claim C104 is supported by SBFSEM observations. However, claims C105-C107 involve speculative interpretations about the fate of daughter cells and the nature of the divisions. While the observations are accurate and the analogies to other kinetoplastids (C105) are appropriate, the actual fate of daughter cells and the mechanisms involved require further investigation.

result: Sexual recombination in Leishmania occurs in the sand fly, and the close positioning of attached haptomonads may facilitate cell fusion events.
evaluation: Claim C109 is established knowledge supported by multiple citations. However, claim C110 is speculative inference based on spatial organization. While the hypothesis is reasonable, no direct evidence of cell fusion events or sexual recombination at the haptomonad stage is provided in this study.

result: A model of Leishmania adhesion was developed combining in vivo and in vitro observations. Promastigotes explore surfaces with their flagella, and if suitable positions are found, adhesion is triggered with calcium potentially playing a role. Initial adhesion stages are reversible, but a point of no return occurs. Adhesion continues with axoneme and PFR disassembly, flagellar membrane expansion, and attachment plaque assembly. Mature cells orient orthogonally to the surface. Haptomonads can divide slowly, potentially generating attached and unattached forms. Detached cells with attachment plaques may represent early differentiation to free-swimming forms. In vitro metacyclics are not adhesion competent, and laterally attached cells may represent transitional forms.
evaluation: Claims C111-C120 represent a comprehensive model integrating multiple observations. While many components are well-supported (e.g., C111, C115, C116 based on direct observations), several aspects are speculative (e.g., C112 about calcium's role, C117 about asymmetric division, C118 about detached cells, C120 about laterally attached cells). The model appropriately acknowledges uncertainties and caveats about in vitro vs. in vivo differences. This represents a valuable synthesis but requires further experimental validation of speculative components.

result: The detailed 3D organization and architecture of haptomonad attachment revealed in this study will facilitate future work on identifying proteins involved in adhesion and understanding the mechanism and role of haptomonad attachment in the Leishmania life cycle.
evaluation: Claim C121 is a reasonable forward-looking statement about the implications of the study. The detailed structural characterization provided does establish a foundation for future molecular and functional studies, though the actual utility will depend on subsequent research.
